item.title: Wrangling Two Monsters Part II: TDD with PICO C/C++ SDK in a Nutshell
item.description:
Intro

In part I, we’ve addressed the first monter, setting up a CMake project for TDD with Pico C/C++ SDK. This article will attempt to wrangle the second monster, the PICO C/C++ SDK itself

TDD Setup Overview

  • terms:

    • host build: code compiler for your development architecture (Your dev laptop)
    • target build: code compiler for the Pico board
    • target: generic reference for which platform the project is built
    • CMake target (for the purpose of this article): an item which will be produced by CMake build system
    • listfile: file containing CMake language

  • All development will be done in a Debian container

item.title: Wrangling Two Monsters Part I: CMake and Pico C/C++ SDK Setup for TDD
item.description:
Intro

Embedded world is a tedious place. The best way to navigate it while keeping your sanity is through the practice of Test Driven Development (TDD).

Being a bit blunt, Pico C/C++ SDK is a monstrosity (huge codebase with nested projects) managed by another monstrosity (CMake).

Nevertheless, both can be dealt with by using the popular strategy of “How to eat an elephant” - one small piece at a time.

item.title: My MacDventure Part 2: Burning ISOs on a Mac
item.description:
Burning ISOs On A Mac

Intro

So there I was again trying to feel at home on the Mac.

The biggest challenge with migrating from Linux to Mac is the lack of tools and ways to do things that are taken for granted on a Linux system.

For example the popular gpg command line tool is not present on the Mac.

So, your typical workflows, such as downloading and validating an ISO, are very likely to be derailed.

item.title: My MacDventure Part 1: Setting Up Container-based C/C++ development Environment
item.description:
So there I was, with the gift of a brand new MacBook Air. Over the past
decade and a half, my primary daily drivers have ALL been Linux.

However, recently I decided to try something new. That something new
involved getting a MacBook Air.

I’ve been looking for a good coding platform, and most of the professional
software engineers I know RAVE about how great Macs are. Well, Macs are
Unix after all, and Unix is very similar to Linux. Therefore, I should be
right at home. What could go wrong? Right????
